lesson.title: Reversing the Cosecant Rule: The Integral of csc(x)cot(x)
lesson.summary: Just as sec(x)*tan(x) integrates back to sec(x), its co-function partner csc(x)*cot(x) integrates to -csc(x), the sign flip coming straight from the derivative of csc(x).
lesson.body:
The integral of csc(x)*cot(x) is: integral of csc(x)*cot(x) dx = -csc(x) + C.

This rule follows from the derivative of cosecant: the derivative of csc(x) is -csc(x)*cot(x). Differentiate the candidate antiderivative -csc(x) to check it: the derivative of -csc(x) is -(-csc(x)*cot(x)), which simplifies to csc(x)*cot(x). Since differentiating -csc(x) produces exactly csc(x)*cot(x), -csc(x) is an antiderivative of csc(x)*cot(x), confirming the rule.

This is the sixth and final rule in the basic trig integral family previewed earlier in this unit. Stepping back, a clean pattern ties all six together: whenever the paired derivative involves a co- function, cosine, cotangent, or cosecant, a negative sign appears, and that negative sign has to be canceled by negating the antiderivative itself. That is why integral of sin(x) dx = -cos(x) + C and integral of csc^2(x) dx = -cot(x) + C and integral of csc(x)*cot(x) dx = -csc(x) + C all carry a minus sign, while their non co- partners, integral of cos(x) dx = sin(x) + C, integral of sec^2(x) dx = tan(x) + C, and integral of sec(x)*tan(x) dx = sec(x) + C, do not.

Worked example: find integral of 2*csc(x)*cot(x) dx. Pull out the constant: 2 * integral of csc(x)*cot(x) dx = 2*(-csc(x)) + C = -2*csc(x) + C. Verify by differentiating: the derivative of -2*csc(x) is -2*(-csc(x)*cot(x)) = 2*csc(x)*cot(x), which matches the original integrand.

As before, csc(x) and cot(x) are undefined at integer multiples of pi, so the rule applies on any interval avoiding those points.
